decisions.question: What decision is this system supposed to support: publishing a line, pricing a bet, or ranking strategies?
decisions.matters: The three goals need different evidence. A published line needs calibration; a priced bet needs a beatable market; a leaderboard needs a fair comparison rule. Optimising for one silently breaks the others.
decisions.have: The brief states two goals: originate own NFL lines, and run a leaderboard competition with rewards. Earlier sessions built both, plus a correlation lab and a prop framework.
decisions.lack: No stated use: research, recreational betting, or a commercial product. No stated stake size, bankroll, jurisdiction or risk limit.
decisions.changes: A one-line statement of intended use and whether real money is involved.
decisions.discovery: Ask for the use in one sentence, then re-derive the pass/fail bar from it. Until then the dashboard keeps the strictest bar (no strategy published as profitable).

decisions.question: Is real money at stake, and under which jurisdiction's rules?
decisions.matters: Rewards, execution, advertising and data use all depend on it. Several operators restrict or void bets placed on obviously erroneous prices, and reward pools can be regulated.
decisions.have: An official NFL responsible-betting article documenting the league's own $6.2m programme. Operator house rules for settlement.
decisions.lack: No jurisdiction, operator account, licence or stake information for this project. The repository is a research sample only.
decisions.changes: A named jurisdiction and operator. This is a legal question, not a data question.
decisions.discovery: Do not guess. If real money is intended, get the governing rules for that jurisdiction before any execution feature is built.

decisions.question: What counts as success: return on investment, closing-line value, or forecast calibration?
decisions.matters: ROI needs hundreds of settled bets to separate from luck. CLV needs an opening-line archive. Calibration needs only prices and outcomes. They rank strategies differently.
decisions.have: A pre-registered eight-gate scheme in which G8 uses a shrunk ROI with a 0.5% economic bar. A measured no-skill band for eleven strategies.
decisions.lack: No stated objective function from the owner, and no opening-line archive before 2021, which rules out a full-history CLV study.
decisions.answer: Provisional: rank on shrunk ROI, and report CLV and calibration alongside it. Status is provisional because the owner has not chosen.
decisions.changes: An owner decision on the primary metric, plus an opening-line source if CLV is chosen.
decisions.discovery: Run the three metrics side by side on the existing ledger (cheap: the data is already there) and see whether the ranking actually changes before choosing.

decisions.question: How often must the numbers refresh, and who refreshes them?
decisions.matters: An injury-based view is worthless if it is stale. A weekly cadence and a named owner are the difference between a dashboard and a museum.
decisions.have: A committed snapshot dated 2026-11-12 and a deterministic rebuild with no network access.
decisions.lack: No scheduler, no credentialled data source, and no named maintainer. Nothing in this repository refreshes itself.
decisions.changes: A cadence and a person. Without a named owner, every number on the site is a snapshot and should be labelled with its date.
decisions.discovery: Time-box a manual weekly refresh first; only automate once the manual loop has run four weeks without a miss.

decisions.question: May this repository copy NFL-published injury data into its own files?
decisions.matters: This decides whether the injury work can be a database or must stay a citation.
decisions.have: The official NFL Terms: section 1.1 prohibits copying, reproducing or distributing the Services' contents, and section 1.3 prohibits systematic retrieval to compile a collection or database without express prior written consent.
decisions.lack: No written permission from the NFL. No legal review.
decisions.answer: No for bulk redistribution. The safe pattern used here is: link every row to the official page, transcribe only what is needed to verify a specific published claim, keep it minimal, and never present it as a substitute for the official report.
decisions.changes: Written consent from the NFL would change it. Nothing else would.
decisions.discovery: If bulk historical injury data is needed, request it in writing rather than scraping it.

decisions.question: Is there an official machine-readable injury feed?
decisions.matters: A feed makes refresh automatable and auditable. A web page makes it manual and fragile.
decisions.have: Durable per-week official pages, e.g. a 2025 week-10 page and a 2026 week-10 page, each rendering the full report. Roster-move pages are also durable by month.
decisions.lack: No documented public API or bulk export. Nothing on the pages promises stability of the format.
decisions.answer: No documented public feed was found. The durable per-week URL is the best official anchor available, and it is what this dashboard cites.
decisions.changes: An official data licence or API would change it. A third-party mirror does not, because it cannot be verified as official.
decisions.discovery: Link-check the durable URLs each week. If one 404s, the row becomes blank and is flagged, rather than being repaired with a mirror.

decisions.question: Is there an official depth chart, so that 2nd, 3rd and 4th string can be identified?
decisions.matters: This is the single biggest blocker in the brief. Without a depth chart there is no official way to say that a backup is playing, so no 'backup deficiency' value can be verified.
decisions.have: Official rosters, which list every player with a position and a roster status. Official injury reports, which give practice and game status per player. Official reserve-list and trade pages.
decisions.lack: A working official depth-chart page. The URL this session tried returned HTTP 404 on 2026-11-12. No club-published depth chart was verified either.
decisions.answer: No. 2nd/3rd/4th-string identification cannot be verified from an official source today, so every string-level value on this site is left blank and flagged.
decisions.changes: A working official depth-chart page, a licensed depth feed, or an owner decision to accept a clearly-labelled unofficial source.
decisions.discovery: Re-check the official depth URL each week and record the result. In parallel, build the availability signal from injury designations only, which IS official, and treat depth as a later upgrade.

decisions.question: Are snap counts available from an official source, to measure who actually played?
decisions.matters: Participation is the only way to prove a backup replaced a starter. Injury designations say who might miss the game; snaps say who took the reps.
decisions.have: Official rosters and injury designations. No participation data.
decisions.lack: A working official snap-count page. The Next Gen Stats URLs tried this session returned HTTP 404, so no value is published.
decisions.changes: A working official participation source, or a licensed one.
decisions.discovery: Probe the official stats endpoints weekly and log the result. Do not substitute an unofficial participation file without labelling it.

decisions.question: Are the market prices in this repository official?
decisions.matters: Every ROI, correlation and gate result depends on the prices. If the prices are unofficial, every derived number is reproducible but not verifiable.
decisions.have: A pinned, checksummed third-party dataset, plus operator pages that define how prices settle.
decisions.lack: A licensed official quote archive with timestamps. No official publisher distributes historical NFL prices.
decisions.answer: No. The dataset is third-party. Every price-derived number is labelled RECOMPUTED, never OFFICIAL, and this is why the strict gates refuse to certify an edge.
decisions.changes: A licensed feed would change it, and nothing else would.
decisions.discovery: Before spending on a feed, check whether the conclusion even depends on price precision: the correlation result is near zero with a confidence interval that excludes anything exploitable.

decisions.question: Does injury and availability information actually beat the closing line?
decisions.matters: This is the whole commercial question. If it does not, the injury tracking is a monitoring tool, not a betting edge.
decisions.have: A 254-player official availability snapshot for one week, an eight-gate protocol that already rejects every strategy tested, and a measured no-skill band.
decisions.lack: A historical injury archive aligned to games. Without it, the hypothesis cannot be backtested at all, so there is exactly one week of evidence and zero test results.
decisions.changes: A historical injury file of at least five seasons, plus a pre-registered rule. Until then the honest answer is 'unknown'.
decisions.discovery: Pre-register the rule and the pass bar BEFORE looking at the historical data. Then acquire the data. Reversing that order is how every false edge in this repository was created.

decisions.question: How many settled bets are needed before a strategy can be ranked at all?
decisions.matters: A leaderboard that ranks on 50 bets ranks luck. The published power calculation already shows the observed edges need hundreds to hundreds of thousands of bets.
decisions.have: A published table of bets needed at the observed and shrunk edges: from 843 up to more than 393,000 for the rules tested. Gate G1 requires 200 overall and 100 in confirmation.
decisions.lack: No season-long or multi-season sample for any candidate rule that clears the bar, and no statement of how many seasons the owner is willing to wait.
decisions.answer: At least one full season of pre-registered, out-of-sample bets before a rank is published; the power table is the per-rule number and it is usually larger than one season.
decisions.changes: A larger sample, or a much larger true edge.
decisions.discovery: Publish the required sample next to every rank, so a reader can see how thin the evidence is rather than trusting a position on a list.

decisions.question: Which metric should the leaderboard actually sort on?
decisions.matters: Sorting on raw ROI rewards the luckiest rule. Sorting on a shrunk measure rewards the most credible one. They are different competitions.
decisions.have: Four candidate measures in the existing evaluation: raw ROI, week-block bootstrap interval, permutation percentile, and empirical-Bayes shrunk ROI. Leagues already use a draft order for tied records as an official tiebreak analogy.
decisions.lack: An owner decision, and a written tiebreak rule for the leaderboard.
decisions.answer: Provisional: shrunk ROI as the primary sort, with the permutation percentile as a tiebreak and the sample size always displayed.
decisions.changes: An owner decision after seeing the three rankings side by side.
decisions.discovery: Compute all three rankings on the existing ledger and publish the disagreement. If the top three differ, the choice matters and deserves an explicit rule.

decisions.question: How should the many-rules problem be handled?
decisions.matters: Testing 18 rules and reporting the best one guarantees an impressive-looking winner even when none has skill. The official statistics guidance is explicit that post-hoc pairwise comparison does not work.
decisions.have: Benjamini-Hochberg control at q <= 0.10 across the whole family, applied in the existing gates.
decisions.lack: A timestamped pre-registration of each rule before its test, visible in the repository history.
decisions.answer: Keep BH-FDR, and add a pre-registration commit hash per rule so the test order cannot be quietly revised.
decisions.changes: Nothing; this is a methodological standard rather than a preference.
decisions.discovery: Add the pre-registration hash to the strategy record and make the build fail if a rule has no registration commit.

decisions.question: Are same-game combinations correlated enough to price a parlay differently?
decisions.matters: If they are, parlays can be positive expected value. If they are not, parlays only compound the margin.
decisions.have: A measured spread-by-total correlation of +0.0086 with a 95% interval from -0.0162 to +0.0332 over 6,784 settled games, reproduced independently in this session. A break-even requirement of phi >= 0.0975 for two legs at -110.
decisions.lack: Any measured pair that clears the requirement and is not already re-priced by the operator.
decisions.answer: No for spread-by-total. The measured value is an order of magnitude below the requirement, and the interval excludes it.
decisions.changes: A different leg pair measured on the same protocol, e.g. player-level pairs, which need a prop-line archive this repository does not have.
decisions.discovery: Measure player-level pairs only after a prop-line source exists. Otherwise the conclusion is already firm for the market pairs that can be measured.

decisions.question: What does the official injury report actually tell us, and what does it not?
decisions.matters: It is the one availability source that IS official, so its limits define what can be claimed.
decisions.have: The official policy text: practice report uses Did Not Participate, Limited Participation (less than 100% of normal repetitions) and Full Participation (100%). Game status uses Questionable (uncertain), Doubtful (unlikely) and Out (will not play). 'Probable' was removed. A player certain to play is not listed on the game status report at all.
decisions.lack: Final inactive lists in machine-readable form, and any severity measure. The free-text injury column is blank on most rows.
decisions.answer: It supports a three-level availability signal (out / doubtful / questionable) plus a practice signal. It does NOT support a severity score or a probability of playing.
decisions.changes: Nothing; this is the official definition.
decisions.discovery: Never convert 'questionable' into a percentage. The policy says uncertain, and the 50% reading is a betting convention, not an official number.

decisions.question: How should a backup-deficiency value be defined while depth charts are unavailable?
decisions.matters: The brief asks specifically about 2nd/3rd/4th string replacements. Without depth data the concept cannot be measured, so any number would be invented.
decisions.have: Two official signals per player: a game status and a practice status, plus a roster status. Enough to build a per-club, per-unit availability-stress index with declared weights.
decisions.lack: Depth order. There is no official field that says a player is second string.
decisions.answer: Publish two layers and never mix them: an OFFICIAL availability layer built from injury designations, and a DEPTH layer that stays blank until a source exists. The index on this site is the official layer only.
decisions.changes: A verified depth source would allow a genuine starter-versus-backup split.
decisions.discovery: Ask each club's own site whether it publishes a depth chart, and record the result per club, rather than assuming a league-wide page exists.

decisions.question: What happens when an official page changes or disappears?
decisions.matters: A citation that no longer resolves is not evidence. The site currently links 1,000+ official URLs.
decisions.have: Committed JSON snapshots of what was read, dated, with the exact statement each source supports. A build gate that fails if any link is missing from the source register.
decisions.lack: Resolvable web archives for every source, and an automated link-rot check against the live web.
decisions.answer: Snapshot the statement, not just the URL, and date it. If the page changes, the snapshot still shows what was read on that date.
decisions.changes: Nothing; this is the durable pattern.
decisions.discovery: Add a monthly link check that records HTTP status per source, without failing the build when an external site is down.

decisions.question: Who funds the rewards, and under what terms?
decisions.matters: The brief asks for a leaderboard competition with rewards. Rewards create obligations: eligibility, payout, disputes, and in some jurisdictions a licence.
decisions.have: A written leaderboard specification and a reward-eligibility bar that requires every gate to pass.
decisions.lack: A pool, a sponsor, a currency, payout terms, an eligibility rule and a jurisdiction.
decisions.answer: No reward can be promised. The competition is currently a specification with zero eligible entrants.
decisions.changes: A funded pool and written terms.
decisions.discovery: Either fund it explicitly and publish the terms, or drop the word 'reward' and run it as a reputation-only leaderboard. A half-promised reward is worse than none.

decisions.question: Can the existing results be reproduced by someone who does not trust the pipeline?
decisions.matters: If not, none of it is evidence. This session tested exactly this.
decisions.have: An independent recomputation of 14 published numbers using hand-written arithmetic rather than the producing pipeline, all reproducing. Two data-layout defects were found in the process.
decisions.lack: A second independent implementation of the model itself, as opposed to the summary statistics.
decisions.answer: The published summary statistics reproduce exactly. The model that produced the input table has not been independently reimplemented.
decisions.changes: A clean-room reimplementation of the line-origination model.
decisions.discovery: Port the model to a second implementation and require agreement to a stated tolerance before publishing any model result as a finding.

decisions.question: Is the 2026 season sample usable?
decisions.matters: The season is live. Using partial-season results invites look-ahead and small-sample errors.
decisions.have: A live snapshot, clearly dated, and an explicit rule that unplayed fixtures are excluded from calculations.
decisions.lack: A completed season, and any injury archive for completed games.
decisions.answer: Use 2026 only for the current availability snapshot. Do not compute strategy statistics on it.
decisions.changes: Season completion.
decisions.discovery: Keep the snapshot date on every page, and refuse to publish a 2026 ROI.
